abstract: Chromatin mobility, the exploration of 3D conformations by the chromatin fibre, is implicated in transcription and DNA repair, and is thought to decrease progressively as cells differentiate. Here, combining live-cell 3D single-nucleosome tracking with genomic approaches, we show that chromatin mobility instead changes in a cell-type-specific manner, increasing as pluripotent cells acquire posterior fates. This is accompanied by 3D genome reorganisation, including loss of Polycomb-associated interactions and emergence of CDX2-associated interactions. Withdrawal of posteriorising WNT/{beta}-catenin signalling rapidly reduces chromatin mobility and partially restores Polycomb-associated chromatin interactions, while Cdx1/2/4-null cells fail to acquire these WNT/{beta}-catenin-dependent changes. Together, our findings establish chromatin mobility as a regulated property of cell state, with WNT/{beta}-catenin signalling and CDX factors acting as mediators that fine-tune the sampling of 3D chromatin interactions during cell state transitions.
